messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Vignette:
Renée Calloway is a 50-year-old single jeweler of mixed North American heritage who was referred for psychological assessment following a physical and sexual assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 54, indicating severe posttraumatic stress, and has only recently acknowledged to herself that she needs professional help.

The assault took place on a Thursday evening after Renée had stayed late to finish a custom commission at the small independent jewelry studio she has owned and operated for nearly two decades. A man she recognized as a former occasional customer — someone who had come in twice to have a watch repaired — entered the studio just as she was locking up. What followed was a prolonged assault during which he restrained her against the workbench where she cuts and sets stones. The assault ended only when a passing delivery driver knocked at the glass door. The attacker left through the back. Renée was left on the floor of her own studio, surrounded by the tools of her trade, the half-finished commission still under the loupe on her bench.

In the weeks that followed, Renée's memory of the event took on a fractured, unreliable quality that she found deeply disorienting. Certain moments are etched with unbearable precision — the particular smell of the man's jacket, the sensation of the metal edge of the workbench against her back — while other stretches of the assault are entirely blank, as though the tape had been cut. When fragments surface without warning, they arrive mid-thought and then vanish before she can examine them, leaving her shaken and disoriented. She has found herself stopping the memory deliberately whenever it begins to unspool, pressing it back before it can reach its fullest extent. What frightened her most about this was not the remembering itself but the blanks — she had come to believe that the gaps meant something worse had happened than she could consciously hold, and that if she ever let the memory run its full course, she would not survive what she found there.

The physical sensation of nausea has become one of the most reliable signals that her body is registering something her mind has not yet caught up to. It arrives without obvious cause — at the grocery store, in traffic — and by the time she identifies it as connected to the assault, the moment has already reorganized her entire day around managing it. On two occasions she has seen the attacker at a distance in her neighborhood, and both times she was unable to return to work that day. Talk of loss among colleagues or clients — someone mentioning a death, a bereavement — produces a visceral response she cannot easily explain to others and has stopped trying to.

Renée now enters every room — her studio, a restaurant, the post office — with her attention moving immediately to the exits. She has come to feel safe in only a handful of places: her apartment, her car, and one friend's home. Strangers who approach her in ordinary contexts, a man asking directions, a customer stepping too quickly toward the counter, register to her as immediate threats requiring assessment. At work, this has had concrete consequences. She has stopped accepting walk-in clients entirely, citing appointment-only hours she invented after the assault, and she has had to turn away several long-standing customers who noticed the change and did not return. The studio, once a source of deep professional pride, now feels like a place she endures rather than inhabits.

What troubles Renée as much as any of this is what she has come to believe about herself in the aftermath. She had always thought of herself as capable and self-sufficient, and the fact that she has not simply moved past this event reads to her as evidence that she is a lousy coper — that other people would have managed better, recovered faster, resumed their lives more completely. She describes feeling dirty in a way that ordinary hygiene cannot address, a sense that something about her is permanently altered and marked. Most of the time she feels nothing at all — a flatness she describes as feeling dead inside, which she finds almost more disturbing than grief would be.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when a longtime client, a woman she has known for years, came in to collect a repaired necklace and mentioned offhandedly that her husband had just died. Renée excused herself to the back room and could not stop shaking for twenty minutes. She booked the appointment that afternoon. She is not sure what she hopes for, but she knows she cannot continue to disappear from her own life.
